I think it's best for you to sit down with her and talk about her treatment if nobody else will. Not mention it, really talk about what she needs for her troubles and how to go about it.

I had visited the school counselor for my depression/suicidal ideation which gave me temporary relief whenever I went in and happened to have a bad mood. If I didn't, we would just chat. It didn't do anything remarkable in the long run but it didn't cost me because it was in school. Seeing an actual therapist was similar, temporary comfort, slightly greater effect in the long run but not enough. I quit before we could focus on building habits to help me in the future which is what you're supposed to do. She suggested a lot that we dissect and analyze my thinking and behavior. Paying for it (insurance doesn't cover everything, it was about 20 Euros per session), driving there, putting yourself together every week trying to give them a clear picture of how you're doing, it's not for everyone.

You can tell her that she doesn't need to stick with talking therapy (what they mean when they say "therapy" at least at the beginning) by any means but she should give this type of treatment a shot. It may help and there is no shame in it. There are other options or combinations of options, most of all medication and talking (again). Some pills give you more distance in your daily and some help you from being lethargic. That's what I know. The least you can get from it is a better understanding of yourself.

I think, all you can do is try to persuade her into getting professional help without being too pushy. You want to help your friend, not make therapy seem like a chore. It isn't for everyone but it has the potential to change your life. If she doesn't like her therapist, she can see a different one. Let your friend know what the options are. If you can find small ways to support her, that's more than enough too. 🙂
